title: Anti-Monopolists Soared in the Midterms. You Can Help With What's Next.
author: Lee Hepner
content:
Yesterday, the results came in for one of the most significant elections in
our lifetimes, one which may mark the end of an era. I want to offer an
analysis of what happened, not from a standard partisan or political
perspective, but with the goal of explaining how this election is going to
change corporate behavior, and, more importantly, how you might be able get
involved.

Why is it so important to be involved in governing? To understand that, let's
examine what happened yesterday, its consequences in corporate America, and
how governing intersects with politics.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ibvz!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-

media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F884cd15a-fee6-4b2e-bae0-f63509325621_996x760.png)

  1. **How significant are the results?**

It's hard to overstate what happened. The actual victory for Democrats, or
loss for Republicans depending on how you see it, was so crushing it was on
the [scale](https://dsl.richmond.edu/panorama/congress/map/1974) of 1974, the
electoral reaction to Watergate. It's so big that the concept of "red" and
"blue" states, which [comes out](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/when-
republicans-became-red-democrats-became-blue-104176297/) of the 2000 election,
might be over. The Democrats not only won the U.S. Senate, taking seats in
places like Kansas, Iowa, and perhaps even Alaska and Mississippi, they
flipped every statewide seat and both legislative chambers in Texas. They
literally do not have enough staffers for the seats they now occupy.

It's like 1974 in another way too. Unlike earlier wave elections, like 1982,
2006, and 2018, this one seems ideological. That is, the new crop of Democrats
have fundamentally different beliefs about the world than the incumbents. As
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa argued, the core question is no longer
progressive cultural politics, it's economic power. To pick another race, you
could look at the Texas Attorney General candidate, Nathan Johnson, who won
his election on an [explicit](https://kvia.com/voter-guide-2026/texas-
attorney-general/2026/10/07/nathan-johnson-candidate-for-texas-attorney-
general/) consumer protection and antimonopoly platform.

In that sense, it's more akin to the Watergate Babies on the left who ditched
Wright Patman, or the Gingrich revolution on the right who got rid of the
moderate Republicans in 1994.

This vote was clearly driven by anger at Donald Trump. The Iran War is deeply
[unpopular](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/10/08/iran-conflict-
remains-deeply-unpopular-as-many-americans-expect-it-to-go-on-for-months/),
and 73% of all voters link the conflict to persistently high gas and fuel
prices. Heading into the final month of the midterm elections, some 75% of
Americans were concerned about the rising cost of food and groceries. While
Trump has tried to wrangle the economy with tariffs, voters overwhelmingly
[link](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/10/us-voters-are-angry-tariffs-and-
war-midterms-wont-bring-quick-change) tariffs to higher prices.

But there are other issues as well. Favorability toward the United States'
ongoing support for Israel has also
[plummeted](https://globalaffairs.org/research/public-opinion-survey/american-
favorability-israel-drops-record-low) among Democrats and Independents, and is
declining among Republicans. On Election Day, Trump announced the government
would be [ending](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/03/politics/trump-us-aid-israel)
its $4 billion per year in military support for Israel by the end of 2026.

In essence, corporate power and the national security posture of the U.S. were
both on the ballot. That is unusual and speaks to a broader mandate than just
an angry anti-Trump vote.

  2. **How can I help?**

If you are interested in governing in this new environment, please submit your
resume to the [resume bank](https://www.economicliberties.us/resume-bank/)
that my organization, the American Economic Liberties Project, set up. There
are going to be thousands of open slots for policymaking, communications,
legal and investigative positions, across the country, and we are trying to
find people who care about monopoly power to staff the newly elected political
leaders and help them enact their agenda. So if you're interested, please
upload your details [here](https://www.economicliberties.us/resume-bank/).

  3. **How is Wall Street responding?**

Already, we're seeing the stock market manifest changes in capital flows. The
stock market is surprisingly up; oil prices have
[crashed](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/oil-price-iran-war-us-election-
strait-hormuz.html) as traders expect Trump to wind down the conflict, and
much of the market is up on the notion that "gridlock" will mean higher
corporate profits and lower tariffs. Companies that offer Medicaid services
[increased](https://www.beckershospitalreview.com/finance/post-midterm-
healthcare-stock-report/) in value, companies that offer privatized Medicare
are [lower](https://www.marketwatch.com/story/hospital-stocks-rally-while-
drugmakers-brace-for-scrutiny-heres-what-the-democratic-wave-means-for-
healthcare-625b79f3), the data center build-out world is [taking a
hit](https://x.com/LeifInvests/status/2118018354246201629?s=20) as financing
and permitting costs are set to increase, but those who already have data
centers, namely the big tech hyperscalers, have done [quite
well](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/04/apple-and-other-big-tech-stocks-surge-
after-2026-midterm-elections.html).

[![Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QZt-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe5c12c8-8df7-456f-a9fd-079b0a71b8d7_1150x2048.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QZt-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe5c12c8-8df7-456f-a9fd-079b0a71b8d7_1150x2048.jpeg)Companies
involved in the data center buildout are reflecting the midterm mandate.

The new political environment has already had one significant consequence in
the corporate world: the biggest break-up of the century so far. The $400
billion corporation CVS, which owns insurer giant Aetna and PBM Caremark, just
[announced](https://www.reuters.com/legal/transactional/cvs-health-split-two-
separating-pharmacy-business-insurance-2026-11-04/) it is preemptively
splitting itself apart, in part due to the campaign to break up big medicine
that BIG and all of you helped launch.

Here's how it happened. Since 2016, pharmacy benefit managers have gotten more
and more unpopular, especially since they are owned by insurers and pharmacy
giants who use them to dispense medication in ways that prioritize profits
over care. BIG covered CVS over the years, starting in 2020 with our piece
"[How CVS Became a Health Care Tyrant](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/how-
cvs-became-a-health-care-tyrant)."

Over the past few years, several states, including Arkansas and Tennessee,
passed laws mandating the split up of pharmacies and PBMs. On a Federal level,
Senators Josh Hawley and Elizabeth Warren
[introduced](https://www.warren.senate.gov/news/press-releases/warren-hawley-
introduce-bipartisan-bill-to-break-up-big-medicine/) a similar package of
laws, and newly elected Senators Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Annie Andrews
of South Carolina - both doctors - were on board. The writing was on the wall,
and now CVS is trying to get ahead of the politics by announcing it will be
selling off most of its pharmacy operations. CEO David Joyner explained this
morning that the anticipated regulatory scrutiny is one reason why:

The actual split isn't enough. The conglomerate is trying to keep their
specialty pharmacy that sells the profitable drugs, while splitting off the
less profitable physical pharmacies. But it's a big deal that they are taking
apart their empire. Big medicine is in real trouble.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OkrS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faf0a19fa-7330-44f0-a6bc-2a298f7f3f77_1304x378.png)

  4. **Is this election an endorsement of a Democratic agenda?**

Well, not really, or it's at least yet to be seen. Since 2000, [11 of 13
elections](https://www.mufgamericas.com/sites/default/files/document/2024-11/Consequential-
Elections.pdf) have been "change" elections, meaning there's a change in party
control over the Presidency or at least one of the chambers of Congress.
Voters are angry, and no one in power is doing much to assuage that anger, so
frustrations are wielded against whatever party is in power. Democrats will
soon have power, but they do not necessarily have the enduring trust of the
public.

As I've mentioned in recent columns, that cynicism created a wedge in the
discourse among Democrats, with Senator Schatz and Representative Casar
[squaring
off](https://x.com/RepCasar/status/2116160217884856694?a=PXfHzrjMQcXhdmHEqXY&s=20)
recently over the extent to which Democrats should wield their power. Their
sweeping success in the midterms certainly militates in favor of a mandate for
bold action.

Now that Dems have won that power -- taking back both the Senate and the
House, and many [state offices](https://boondoggle.substack.com/p/the-data-
center-revolt-foretold-the) -- Republicans are due for their own intra-party
reckoning. If there is one certain outcome of the midterms, it's that MAGA is
dead.

  5. **Was this election an endorsement of the fight against oligarchy?**

I think, yes. This was among the most expensive election cycles in American
history, with [$12
billion](https://www.opensecrets.org/news/2026/10/opensecrets-predicts-
record-12-billion-in-midterm-election-spending/) spent. Just 50 individuals
were [responsible](https://www.newsweek.com/the-billionaires-who-spent-won-
and-lost-the-most-at-the-midterms-12661688) for over $2.8 billion of that
spending. In a country of about 343 million citizens, 0.00001458% -- about 15
millionths of a percent -- were responsible for over 23% of all election
spending. And yet, the side with more money did not win.

One of the most notable political figures this cycle is the richest man in the
world, Elon Musk, who cleared every previous record by spending $445.5 million
in a single election cycle. In 2020, Musk moved his residence from California
to Texas amid a clash with state officials. Over the next five years, he moved
Tesla, SpaceX, and X/Twitter with him. He also became highly political,
endorsing Trump, running DOGE, and then spent $190 million to elect Texas
Republicans in the 2026 midterms.

Yet, Texas is the bluest it's been in 40 years. By the end of the election
cycle, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico was running against Texas AG
Ken Paxton on paper, but had focused his rhetorical ire on the richest man in
the world.

Anyone can point to any number of reasons why Democrats in redder areas
prevailed the way they did in these midterms. But to listen to, say, the Texas
Democrats themselves, it was not about alienating voters with partisan
posturing on culture issues, but with the rhetoric of economic populism, and a
unifying "[love thy
neighbor](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/state/texas/2026/11/04/from-
teacher-to-senator-how-talarico-flipped-texas-after-30-years/92608180007/)"
reorientation of politics in the state. It was a plea for moral clarity
against power.

  6. **Did Anti-Monopoly Messaging Factor into the Election?**

Yes. Heading into the elections, I put together a spreadsheet with every
candidate I could find that explicitly ran on an anti-monopoly platform and
came up with 71 legitimate Federal and some state candidates. The lion's share
were Democrat candidates, but there were a couple Republicans, too. And that
was while I was trying to be conservative in my assessments. I'm not alone, it
was fairly common for electoral analysts to notice the [populist
tone](https://www.newyorker.com/news/the-lede/how-democrats-are-reclaiming-
the-politics-of-populism) of the campaigns. One advocacy group
[found](https://www.theverge.com/policy/1026017/democrats-leaned-into-big-
tech-and-ai-opposition-this-cycle) that Democrats spent $29 million on 154 ads
that mentioned "Big Tech."

As a campaign messaging example, Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown won his
race narrowly, [pitching](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/04/data-
centers-are-midterms-big-loser-01145171) to voters, "I do not work for data
centers. I do not work for Wall Street. I work for you."

Elsewhere, I was tracking 41 local ballot measures across the country, in
California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, North Dakota, Ohio and
Wisconsin, regarding whether to allow new construction of data centers. As of
this writing, it would appear that _[every single one](https://dashboard-
production-c2fc.up.railway.app/)_ failed. When data centers are put before
voters, the outcomes aren't even close, with most opposition ending up in the
75-83 percent range.

And these losses weren't due to a bunch of wealthy NIMBYs voting to preserve
property values. In fact, the most damning rebuke came from Downe Township,
New Jersey, an unincorporated community of about 1,400 residents in the
state's poorest county, which voted down a data center measure with 87% of the
vote.

  7. **Did Anti-Monopolists win elected office?**

Yes. I'm not going to go over every candidate I tracked, but here are a few
that you probably didn't see:

  * Josh Turek won his race for Senate in Iowa, flipping a red seat blue, while [campaigning](https://turek4iowa.com/platform/) against vertical integration of healthcare, food price gouging, and private equity ownership of homes and farmland.

  * Ron Sand will lead from the Governor's desk in Iowa, two years after [leading](https://www.bleedingheartland.com/2024/01/30/iowa-state-auditor-asks-feds-to-block-fertilizer-plant-sale/) the effort as State Auditor to block the Koch Industries' acquisition of a fertilizer plant in Lee County. 

  * Sam Forstag will be the first Democrat to win a Montana House seat in 30 years. He campaigned against [meatpacker consolidation](https://nbcmontana.com/news/local/forstag-flint-lay-out-policy-positions-ahead-of-election) and private equity ownership of [mobile home parks](https://dailymontanan.com/2026/10/14/flint-forstag-trade-barbs-during-debate-for-montanas-open-congressional-seat/).

  * Roy Cooper won his "Make Stuff Cost Less" campaign for Senate in North Carolina [pledging](https://roycooper.com/costless/groceries/) to block anti-competitive grocery and food processing mergers and to ban surveillance pricing and price fixing.

  * Antitrust attorney and former Colorado AG Phil Weiser [handily won](https://coloradonewsline.com/2026/11/03/democrat-phil-weiser-elected-colorado-governor/) his bid to become the governor of the state.

  * Melat Kiros won her Congressional seat in Colorado and campaigned [specifically](https://www.cpr.org/2026/05/18/cd-1-race-melat-kiros-democrat-interview/) on the Warren-Hawley Break Up Big Medicine bill.

  * In Georgia, Tanya Miller [won](https://www.tanyaforgeorgia.com/issues) her seat for Attorney General and pledged to "use the full antitrust authority of the office" to address food supply chain issues and ensure greater competition and lower prices.

  * In Arizona, Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill [won](https://www.kjzz.org/elections/2026-10-06/2026-arizona-corporation-commission-race-the-candidates-elex) their statewide election to the state's Corporation Commission, essentially the state's public utilities commission. Both campaigned on making data centers pay their own share of utility utilization, and both criticized excessive utility profits.

  * In Texas, Clayton Tucker declared [victory](https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/politics/election-2026/2026/11/04/566233/democrat-clayton-tucker-wins-texas-agriculture-commissioner-race/) in his bid for statewide Agriculture Commissioner. His campaign included "busting monopolies that dominate the agriculture industry, such as Tyson Foods and John Deere."

  * Aisha Wahab [should win](https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/district-14-congress-results-22497620.php) a full term Congressional seat in California, and has a record in the state legislature of supporting antitrust reform, and going after surveillance pricing and algorithmic price fixing.

  * Will Lawrence won a Congressional seat in Michigan, campaigning [against](https://inthesetimes.com/article/meet-will-lawrence-the-tenant-organizer-running-for-congress-in-a-deep-purple-district) Wall Street landlords and AI data centers.

There are many more, but the point overall is that anti-monopoly showed up in
a way that it really hasn't in a long time. And a lot is [owed
to](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/monopoly-round-up-did-bernie-sanders)
Bernie Sanders and his _Fight Oligarchy_ tour, which for the past two years
has platformed candidates across the country, building the connective tissue
between populist rhetoric, actual governance, and mass politics. My back-of-
napkin calculation shows Sanders' endorsed candidates, well over 50, won over
90% of their races, and about a dozen of them flipped their seats.

  8. **How did big money interests do?**

In 1982, Democrats had a wave year in response to the Ronald Reagan recession,
but the candidates they recruited were Wall Street-friendly types. As a
result, the party turned increasingly towards a finance-first posture.

The 2026 midterms could have seen a similar dynamic. It might have been a
situation where AI companies dominated politics with an endless bankroll, the
same way the crypto billionaires like Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen emerged
just a few years ago, using hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat
populists and [organizing](https://news.bloombergtax.com/financial-
accounting/cryptos-millions-yield-win-as-moreno-takes-ohio-senate-race-1) the
Republican Congress of the last few years. But that didn't happen, as voters
picked the candidates who had less money in an unusually large number of
races.

Instead, as the populist dynamic became more apparent, the pro-AI SuperPAC
Leading the Future, which counted VC billionaire Ron Conway among its major
donors, and perennial political consultant-turned-crypto lobbyist Chris Lehane
among its muscle, [fell apart](https://www.politico.com/newsletters/decoded-
by-politico/2026/10/12/ron-conways-latest-regret-01116022) under the weight of
AI's undeniable want for popularity.

That's not to say that corporate interests have no pull. Far from it. In
California, the attempt to tax billionaire wealth failed among bitter fights
among unions and over $317 million in [opposition
spending](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-24/more-
than-351-million-spent-on-wealth-tax-on-november-ballot) by the state's
billionaire class, and Xavier Becerra will become the new Governor with the
[backing](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-10/special-
interests-spend-millions-boosting-becerra-in-governors-race) of a lot of
corporate support.

More broadly, there's a reason the stock market is up, and that Wall Street
Democrats are on CNBC talking up the
[virtues](https://www.affiliatedpress.org/2026/11/04/squawk-pod-a-blue-
tsunami-maryland-gov-wes-moore-11-04-26-audio-only/) of incoming Speaker
Hakeem Jeffries. Among investors, the
[consensus](https://www.investors.com/news/midterm-election-stock-market-
trump/) is that the high profit share economy will continue.

  9. **Was there a clear victory among the different factions within the Democratic Party?**

Well, not really. While there were plenty of anti-monopoly candidates, there
were also many candidates like Wisconsin Governor-elect David Crowley, a
favorite of Silicon Valley. While many House incumbent Democrats lost in
primaries, not a single incumbent Democrat Senator, with perhaps one
exception, faced a competitive primary challenge. As a result, despite the
large majorities, there is significant disagreement among Democrats over a
host of questions, such as banking rules, AI, tariffs, and corporate power in
general.

It's worth noting the limited reach of another intellectual trend. Last year,
the book _Abundance_ came out, launched from the citadel of liberalism, the
New York Times and the Atlantic. The Ezra Klein-Derek Thompson
[book](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Abundance/Ezra-
Klein/9781668023488), heralded as a "once-in-a-generation, paradigm-shifting
call to renew a politics of plenty," came out in March 2025 and sparked a
deafening and frequently bitter discourse over the future of the Democratic
Party and governance more broadly.

The Abundance proponents argued for supply side increases to address cost
challenges. They broadly emphasized technocratic approaches to delivering
prosperity through the streamlining of permit issuance and stripping of
bureaucratic red tape. But little of their agenda showed up in campaigns. And
in California, the heart of their movement, Prop 45, the statewide ballot
measure to speed up environmental review of "essential projects," is lagging
54-45. It's not that Abundance "failed," but it is an elite persuasion
vehicle, and has not broadened into electoral politics.

  10. **Is there a Mandate? Governing Matters.**

The mandate of this election, if those who are about to wield power will heed
it, is to negotiate a change in course. Some 250 years ago, that negotiation
produced our Constitution. Since, it has produced laws like the Sherman Act,
the Clayton Act, and the Federal Trade Commission Act. Indeed, some of the
most transformational laws in U.S. history -- laws like the Glass-Steagall
Act, the Securities Exchange Act, the National Labor Relations Act, the Social
Security Act, and the Fair Labor Standards Act -- were passed during a brief
span of years following the Great Depression, as part of the New Deal. The
next Congress, and the Congress after it, should aspire to similar
transformative work.

But these laws, as well as the associated executive authority used to enforce
them, came from legislatures who had in-depth knowledge of how our economy
worked and the confidence to govern. Without offering criticism, I'll note
that many of the people who just took office are neophytes to their positions,
and it would be unsurprising if they were skittish about offending the
powerful without having done it before. Many won't have the knowledge or
experience to do so capably or competently. Others will.

America excels at producing leaders, good and bad, from the random clay of its
citizenry. Ten years ago, Zohran Mamdani was a random housing counselor and
hip hop artist. Fifteen years ago, Donald Trump was a real estate developer
and reality TV star. But underneath these characters is a large group of
lawyers, business people, analysts, policymakers, workers, and citizens, who
offer the advice and help to build the kind of society they value. That's
governing. It's a team sport.

And with that, I'll make the pitch, once again, for you to submit your resume
[here](https://www.economicliberties.us/resume-bank/). Or find other ways to
get involved. It took hundreds of thousands of people decades to make the mess
we're in, and it's going to take an equal amount of time and effort to get us
out of it. Governing is hard, it's not particularly well-paid, but it's
incredibly fun and meaningful. So if you want to try, you should. Now is the
moment.
